title: Understanding and Benchmarking the Commonality of Adversarial Examples
abstract: Speech recognition system converts audio into texts by utilizing deep learning algorithms. Numerous works have demonstrated various adversarial example (AE) attacks, i.e., adding carefully-crafted noises can trick the speech recognition system into outputting completely incorrect texts. This paper aims to reveal the distinctive properties of adversarial audio in terms of phonetics. We believe analyzing the distinctive properties is critical in understanding adversarial attacks on ASR models, as well as guiding the generation and defense of AEs. Thus, we aim to answer three questions: (1) What are the distinctive properties of adversarial audio that are common to diverse attacks? (2) How to quantify these distinctive properties? (3) How can we use these properties to improve the security of ASR models? To answer these questions, we perform a large-scale measurement based on acoustic features and statistical analysis. By measuring a total of 612,000 acoustic-statistical feature vectors for 2,400 audio samples, we obtain four insights on the distinctive properties, i.e., filling energy gap, speech-like morphology, disordered signal, and abnormal linguistic pattern. Based on these properties, we design a naturalness score to assess the stealthiness of attacks and propose an adversarial example detector with an average accuracy of 91.1%.

Numerous works have demonstrated various adversarial example (AE) attacks, i.e., adding carefully-crafted noises can trick the speech recognition system into outputting completely incorrect texts. (3) How can we use these properties to improve the security of ASR models? To answer these ques- tions, we perform a large-scale measurement based on acoustic features and statistical analysis. By measuring a total of 612,000 acoustic-statistical feature vectors for 2,400 audio samples, we obtain four insights on the distinctive properties, i.e., filling energy gap, speech-like morphology, disordered signal, and abnormal linguistic pattern. Introduction The Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) system con- verts audio containing human speeches into texts. Recently, deep learning technologies have greatly improved the accu- racy of ASRs, enabling their wide use in voice assistants in smartphones, vehicles, and even in controlling industrial terminals [1]. However, ASR systems are known to be vulnerable to adversarial example (AE) attacks: An AE with carefully-crafted adversarial noise (AN) can trigger the ASR system to output wrong texts [2], compromising the secu- rity of applications with speech recognition by leading to malicious operations of smartphones, cameras, appliances, vehicles, etc. In the past years, numerous works [3-39] have been devoted to generating or defending AEs on a case-by- case basis, focusing on improving the attack or defense *. Numerous adversarial attacks generate various adversarial audio. What are the distinctive properties of adversarial audio common to diverse attacks? How to quantify these distinctive properties? How can we use these properties to improve the security of ASR models? performance. In this paper, we aim to reveal the distinc- tive properties of adversarial audio in terms of phonetics, which widely exist in ANs and AEs but do not appear in benign audios and white noises. Analyzing the distinctive properties of adversarial audio is critical in understanding adversarial attacks on ASR models, as well as guiding the generation and defense of AEs. Particularly, we investigate three questions: • What are the distinctive properties of adversarial audio that are common to diverse attacks? • How to quantify these distinctive properties? • How can we use these properties to improve the secu- rity of ASR models? To answer these questions, we focus on the acoustic features embedded in the adversarial audio and try to ex- tract distinctive properties from it. We choose the acoustic features due to their critical role in phonetics in facilitating characterizing speech. However, an acoustic feature may have tens of thousands of dimensions, which contain re- dundant information and impose an unnecessary burden in extracting commonality. To overcome this problem, we per- form a large-scale measurement based on statistical analysis to extract distinctive properties of adversarial audio. Measurement Methodology. We first introduce sta- tistical features serving to portray the distribution of the acoustic features. Consequently, we design a total of 255 acoustic-statistical features for measuring. Next, to identify commonalities and eliminate bias, we prepare audio for measurements and generate adversarial audio under vari- ous attack configurations, including attack methods, ASR 1665 DOI 10.1109/SP54263.2024.00111 models, and audio samples. Specifically, we select three distinct and representative adversarial attacks, namely Psy- choacoustic Attack [6], C&W Attack [3], and Imperceptible Attack [4]. These attacks employ different, widely-used distance metrics and audibility metrics [3-8, 10, 12-22] in their attack methodologies. Furthermore, these attacks target different ASR models, each exhibiting distinct archi- tectures categorized as (1) traditional model: Kaldi DNN- HMM [40], (2) CTC-based model: DeepSpeech [41], and (3) attention-based model: LAS [42]. Based on 300 original audio samples with diverse speech contents and 300 targeted utterances, we generate AN and AEs, meanwhile generating white noise and selecting benign audio from the VCTK cor- pus as the comparison audio. Note that all adversarial audio and comparison audio are subjected to our measurement analysis. Overall, we measure 255 acoustic-statistical features for 2,400 audio samples with a total of 612,000 feature vectors, ensuring that our findings are independent of specific at- tacks, models, and samples. Finally, we perform a common- ality check on these features to find distinctive properties that widely exist in ANs and AEs but do not appear in benign audios and white noises. Results. Adversarial noise exhibits similar spectrum patterns to humans' speech, but has abnormal properties that don't follow the frequency or time constraints imposed by human physiology and linguistics. The four insights on distinctive properties are detailed below: • Insight 1: Filling Energy Gap. The adversarial noise tends to manifest itself by filling in the energy gaps of the original audio. Specifically, adversarial noise tends to exhibit high energy (1) in the frequency band outside human speaking (i.e., > 1.5kHz) and (2) in the low- energy areas in both the time domain and frequency domain of the original audio. • Insight 2: Speech-like Morphology. Fragments of ad- versarial noise exhibit a similar morphology to human speech in the time-frequency domain. Specifically, the signal of adversarial noise has (1) prominent formant (reflected in width, height, and number of formant) and (2) long temporal correlation. • Insight 3: Disordered Signal. The signals of adver- sarial examples and adversarial noise do not follow the physiological rules of speeches. Specifically, AEs and ANs are (1) discontinuity and (2) irregularity in the time-frequency domain. • Insight 4: Abnormal Linguistic Pattern. The adver- sarial examples do not follow the linguistic rules of speeches. Specifically, AEs have (1) long duration and (2) long intervals of phonetic units. With the above four insights, we design a naturalness score to assess the difference between AEs and normal speech, indicating the stealthiness of the attack. Based on it, we propose an AE detector and test it using 6 adversarial attacks, including 2 trained and 4 untrained attacks, and achieve a max detection accuracy of 96.2% and an average detection accuracy of 91.1%. In summary, the contributions of the paper include follows: • We investigate the distinctive properties of adversarial audio in terms of phonetics, which can shed light on understanding how and why AEs work. • We discover 4 types of intrinsic attributes of adversarial audios best revealed by 12 acoustic-statistical features. • With the discovered properties, we propose an AE detector with an average accuracy of 91.1%. 2. Background 2.1. Automatic Speech Recognition Automatic speech recognition (ASR) system transcribes audio into texts via three steps: pre-processing, feature ex- traction, and model-based decoding [2], as shown in Fig. 2. First, the input audio is split into millisecond-level segments called frames, and then frames are filtered and windowed for pre-processing [44]. Next, acoustic features, such as spec- trogram, Filter Bank (Fbank), and Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC), are extracted from the frame-level audio. Finally, the acoustic features are fed into decoding models comprising an acoustic model and a language model, where the acoustic model classifies the acoustic features into basic language units, such as characters or phones, and the language model further converts these basic language units into complete words or sentences [2]. 2.2. Adversarial Attacks against ASR Systems Adversarial attacks against speech recognition involve the addition of malicious perturbations to input audio, result- ing in ASR systems transcribing audio into texts that differ from human perception [3]. The key to adversarial attacks is constructing a perturbation making the audio recognized as the target utterance while having low audibility, i.e., gen- erating adversarial examples (AEs). Researchers commonly solve this task as an optimization problem [4]. They employ metrics measuring the distance between the perturbed audio (i.e., AE) and the target utterance, as well as the audibility of the perturbation. We then minimize these metrics by gradient descent methods, referred to white-box attacks. Numerous studies have focused on white-box attacks, with the goal of developing effective metrics for measuring distance and audibility [3, 4, 6, 12, 16, 20].
